claim: Diploid transgenic organisms are either hemi- or homozygous.
source: Diploid transgenic organisms are either hemi- or homozygous.
evidence: This is a statement of established genetic knowledge about diploid organisms.

claim: Genetic assays are required to identify the genotype of diploid transgenic organisms.
source: Genetic assays are, therefore, required to identify the genotype.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of diploid organisms being hemi- or homozygous, reflecting standard practice in the field.

claim: The AGameOfClones vector concept uses two clearly distinguishable transformation markers embedded in interweaved, but incompatible Lox site pairs.
source: Our AGameOfClones vector concept uses two clearly distinguishable transformation markers embedded in interweaved, but incompatible Lox site pairs.
evidence: This describes the design of the vector system developed in this study.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination leads to hemizygous individuals that carry only one marker.
source: Cre-mediated recombination leads to hemizygous individuals that carry only one marker.
evidence: This describes the mechanism and outcome of the AGOC system as designed and tested.

claim: Heterozygous descendants are identified by the presence of both markers.
source: In the following generation, heterozygous descendants are identified by the presence of both markers and produce homozygous progeny that are selected by the lack of one marker.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic identification method used in the AGOC system.

claim: Homozygous progeny are selected by the lack of one marker.
source: In the following generation, heterozygous descendants are identified by the presence of both markers and produce homozygous progeny that are selected by the lack of one marker.
evidence: This describes the selection method for homozygous individuals in the AGOC system.

claim: The AGOC concept was proven in Tribolium castaneum by systematically creating multiple functional homozygous transgenic lines.
source: We prove our concept in Tribolium castaneum by systematically creating multiple functional homozygous transgenic lines suitable for long-term fluorescence live imaging.
evidence: This is the main experimental result of the study, supported by data in tables and figures.

claim: The AGOC approach saves resources and simplifies transgenic organism handling.
source: Our approach saves resources and simplifies transgenic organism handling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results and comparison with traditional methods.

claim: The AGOC concept is expected to work in all diploid model organisms because it relies on the universal Cre-Lox system.
source: Since the concept relies on the universal Cre-Lox system, it is expected to work in all diploid model organisms, for example, insects, zebrafish, rodents and plants.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known universality of the Cre-Lox system across species.

claim: The AGOC concept can be used in knock-out assays to preselect homozygous individuals and minimize the number of wasted animals.
source: With appropriate adaptions, it can be used in knock-out assays to preselect homozygous individuals and thus minimize the number of wasted animals.
evidence: This is a proposed application based on the demonstrated functionality of the system.

claim: Mouse and zebrafish are the most frequently used vertebrate model organisms.
source: The most frequently used vertebrates are mouse and zebrafish.
evidence: This is a statement of common knowledge in the field of model organism research.

claim: Drosophila melanogaster and Tribolium castaneum are the two prevailing insect species used as model organisms.
source: Amongst insects, the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster and the red flour beetle Tribolium castaneum are the two prevailing species.
evidence: This is a statement of common knowledge in the field of insect model organisms.

claim: Transgenesis is the insertion of recombinant DNA into the genome of a model organism.
source: An important standard technique is transgenesis, that is, the insertion of recombinant DNA into the genome of the model organism (Gama Sosa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: Model organisms are typically diploid.
source: Since model organisms are typically diploid, the genotype has to be considered, which leads to a certain experimental complexity.
evidence: This is a statement of biological fact about commonly used model organisms.

claim: Usual mating schemes result in non-transgenic wild-type progeny, hemizygous transgenic progeny, and homozygous transgenic progeny.
source: Usual mating schemes result in (i) non-transgenic wild-type progeny, (ii) hemizygous transgenic progeny, that is, only the maternal or only the paternal chromosome carries the transgene, and (iii) homozygous transgenic progeny, that is, both the maternal and paternal chromosomes carry the transgene.
evidence: This describes the expected Mendelian outcomes of standard transgenic crosses.

claim: Transformation markers can be used to separate wild-type from transgenic individuals, but not hemi- from homozygous individuals.
source: Transformation markers can be used to separate wild-type from transgenic, but not hemi- from homozygous individuals.
evidence: This describes a limitation of traditional transformation marker systems.

claim: Additional experiments are necessary to determine the genotype when transformation markers cannot distinguish between hemizygous and homozygous individuals.
source: Thus, additional experiments are necessary to determine the genotype, for example genetic assays, which are invasive and require manpower as well as consumables.
evidence: This describes the current standard practice and its limitations.

claim: In the AGOC vector concept, all genotypes are directly identifiable by specifically designed distinct phenotypes.
source: In our AGameOfClones (AGOC) vector concept, all genotypes are directly identifiable by specifically designed distinct phenotypes, which permits the systematic creation of homozygous transgenic lines.
evidence: This is a key feature of the AGOC system as demonstrated in the study.

claim: The AGOC approach relies on two clearly distinguishable transformation markers embedded in interweaved, but incompatible Lox site pairs.
source: Our approach relies on two clearly distinguishable transformation markers embedded in interweaved, but incompatible Lox site pairs.
evidence: This describes the molecular design of the AGOC vector system.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination results in hemizygous individuals that retain only one of the two markers.
source: Cre-mediated recombination results in hemizygous individuals that retain only one of the two markers and are thus phenotypically distinguishable from each other and the wild type.
evidence: This describes the mechanism and outcome of the AGOC system.

claim: Hemizygous individuals from Cre-mediated recombination are phenotypically distinguishable from each other and the wild type.
source: Cre-mediated recombination results in hemizygous individuals that retain only one of the two markers and are thus phenotypically distinguishable from each other and the wild type.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic outcome that enables genotype identification.

claim: Descendants that express both markers are identified as heterozygous for the transgene.
source: In the next generation, descendants that express both markers are identified as heterozygous for the transgene.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic identification method for heterozygotes in the AGOC system.

claim: A cross of two heterozygotes results in homozygous progeny that are selected by the lack of one marker.
source: Finally, a cross of two heterozygotes results in homozygous progeny that are selected by the lack of one marker.
evidence: This describes the final step in creating homozygous lines using the AGOC system.

claim: Tribolium castaneum is an emerging insect model organism.
source: The proof-of-principle of the AGOC vector concept relied on the red flour beetle Tribolium castaneum, an emerging insect model organism (Klingler, 2004; Brown et al., 2009), in conjunction with the piggyBac transposon system (Lorenzen et al., 2003; Berghammer et al., 2009), which allows semi-random genomic insertion.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The piggyBac transposon system allows semi-random genomic insertion.
source: The proof-of-principle of the AGOC vector concept relied on the red flour beetle Tribolium castaneum, an emerging insect model organism (Klingler, 2004; Brown et al., 2009), in conjunction with the piggyBac transposon system (Lorenzen et al., 2003; Berghammer et al., 2009), which allows semi-random genomic insertion.
evidence: This is a known characteristic of the piggyBac system, supported by citations.

claim: The pAGOC vector contains mOrange-based and mCherry-based eye-specific transformation markers.
source: We developed the transformation-ready pAGOC vector (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) that contains mOrange-based (Shaner et al., 2008) and mCherry-based (Shaner et al., 2004) eye-specific (Berghammer et al., 1999) transformation markers (mO and mC, respectively).
evidence: This describes the vector design, supported by citations for the fluorescent proteins and promoter.

claim: mOrange and mCherry fluorescent proteins are spectrally separable by appropriate excitation bands and emission filters.
source: Both fluorescent proteins are spectrally separable by appropriate excitation bands and emission filters (Shaner et al., 2005).
evidence: This is a known property of these fluorescent proteins, supported by a citation.

claim: Each marker in the pAGOC vector is flanked upstream by a LoxP site and downstream by a LoxN site.
source: Each marker is flanked upstream by a LoxP site (Hamilton and Abremski, 1984) and downstream by a LoxN (Livet et al., 2007) site, resulting in interweaved Lox site pairs (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the vector design, supported by citations and shown in Figure 1.

claim: LoxP and LoxN sites are incompatible with each other due to variations in the spacer sequences.
source: Due to variations in the spacer sequences, LoxP and LoxN sites are incompatible with each other.
evidence: This is a known property of Lox site variants, explaining the mechanism of the AGOC system.

claim: The pAGOC vector was injected together with a piggyBac transposase-expressing helper vector into pre-blastoderm embryos to achieve germline transformation.
source: We injected this vector together with a piggyBac transposase-expressing helper vector (that is, pATub'piggyBac) into pre-blastoderm embryos to achieve germline transformation.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used to create transgenic lines.

claim: Six F2 founder females were found among the progeny of survivors mated with wild types.
source: All survivors, that is, F1 potential mosaics, were mated with wild types and in six of these crosses, at least one F2 (mO-mC) founder female was found among the progeny.
evidence: This reports the experimental outcome of the germline transformation.

claim: For each cross, one founder female was mated with a wild-type male and the progeny were scored to confirm that only a single insertion had occurred.
source: For each cross, one founder female was mated with a wild-type male and the progeny were scored to confirm that only a single insertion had occurred (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure to verify single insertions, with data in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Six proof-of-principle cultures were established, called AGOC #1 to #6.
source: Transgenic descendants were collected to establish six proof-of-principle cultures, which carry the same transgene, but in different genomic locations. These F3 (mO-mC) pre-recombination hemizygous sublines were called AGOC #1 to #6.
evidence: This reports the establishment of the experimental lines.

claim: The six AGOC sublines carry the same transgene but in different genomic locations.
source: Transgenic descendants were collected to establish six proof-of-principle cultures, which carry the same transgene, but in different genomic locations.
evidence: This describes a key characteristic of the experimental lines.

claim: Homozygous viability was roughly estimated by mating two F3 pre-recombination hemizygous siblings and scoring the progeny.
source: To roughly estimate homozygous viability, two F3 (mO-mC) pre-recombination hemizygous siblings were mated and the progeny were scored (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This describes an experimental procedure with results in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The insertion locations of the transgenes were determined in four of the six AGOC sublines.
source: Additionally, the insertion locations of the transgenes were determined in four of the six AGOC sublines (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This reports experimental results documented in Supplementary file 3.

claim: The mating procedure for systematic creation of homozygous transgenic lines spanned four generations.
source: The mating procedure for the systematic creation of homozygous transgenic lines (Figure 2, an comprehensive scheme is provided in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) spanned four generations and involved a transgenic helper line, ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #1.
evidence: This describes the experimental design, illustrated in Figure 2.

claim: The mating procedure involved a transgenic helper line, ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #1.
source: The mating procedure for the systematic creation of homozygous transgenic lines (Figure 2, an comprehensive scheme is provided in Figure 2—figure supplement 1) spanned four generations and involved a transgenic helper line, ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #1.
evidence: This describes a key component of the experimental design.

claim: The ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #1 line expresses a nuclear-localized Cre recombinase under control of the heat shock protein 68b promoter.
source: This line expresses a nuclear-localized Cre recombinase (Peitz et al., 2002) under control of the heat shock protein 68b promoter (Schinko et al., 2012) and carries a mCerulean-based (Markwardt et al., 2011) eye-specific transformation marker (mCe).
evidence: This describes the helper line design, supported by citations.

claim: The ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #1 line carries a mCerulean-based eye-specific transformation marker.
source: This line expresses a nuclear-localized Cre recombinase (Peitz et al., 2002) under control of the heat shock protein 68b promoter (Schinko et al., 2012) and carries a mCerulean-based (Markwardt et al., 2011) eye-specific transformation marker (mCe).
evidence: This describes the helper line design, supported by citations.

claim: The mating procedure was performed with all six AGOC sublines.
source: The procedure was performed with all six AGOC sublines and phenotypically documented for #5 and #6 (Figure 3).
evidence: This reports the scope of the experimental validation.

claim: The mating procedure was phenotypically documented for AGOC sublines #5 and #6.
source: The procedure was performed with all six AGOC sublines and phenotypically documented for #5 and #6 (Figure 3).
evidence: This reports the documentation of experimental results shown in Figure 3.

claim: Throughout all generations, the subline-specific scores matched the expectations.
source: Throughout all generations, the subline-specific scores matched the expectations.
evidence: This summarizes the experimental results across all generations.

claim: No significant differences between the arithmetic means and the theoretical Mendelian ratios were found.
source: No significant differences between the respective arithmetic means and the theoretical Mendelian ratios were found.
evidence: This reports the statistical analysis of the experimental results.

claim: All expected phenotypes and genotypes were found in all generations.
source: Importantly, all expected phenotypes, and thus all expected genotypes, were found in all generations and consequently, F7 (mO/mO) as well as (mC/mC) homozygotes were obtained for all six AGOC sublines.
evidence: This summarizes the successful outcome of the experimental procedure.

claim: F7 homozygotes were obtained for all six AGOC sublines.
source: Importantly, all expected phenotypes, and thus all expected genotypes, were found in all generations and consequently, F7 (mO/mO) as well as (mC/mC) homozygotes were obtained for all six AGOC sublines.
evidence: This reports the successful creation of homozygous lines for all sublines.

claim: The F3 to F7 crossing procedure was successfully conducted with swapped genders for AGOC #5 and #6 sublines.
source: Two controls were performed with the AGOC #5 and #6 sublines to confirm proper function of the AGOC vector concept: The F3 to F7 crossing procedure was successfully conducted with (i) swapped genders (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 5)
evidence: This reports a control experiment with results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Supplementary file 5.

claim: The F3 to F7 crossing procedure was successfully conducted with an alternative helper subline for AGOC #5 and #6.
source: Two controls were performed with the AGOC #5 and #6 sublines to confirm proper function of the AGOC vector concept: The F3 to F7 crossing procedure was successfully conducted with (i) swapped genders (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 5) and (ii) an alternative helper subline (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B, Supplementary file 5), ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #2, which carries the same Cre recombinase-expressing cassette as the #1 subline, but at a different genomic location.
evidence: This reports a control experiment with results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B and Supplementary file 5.

claim: The ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #2 subline carries the same Cre recombinase-expressing cassette as the #1 subline, but at a different genomic location.
source: ICE{HSP68'NLS-Cre} #2, which carries the same Cre recombinase-expressing cassette as the #1 subline, but at a different genomic location.
evidence: This describes a characteristic of the alternative helper line used in control experiments.

claim: Three transformation-ready derivatives were created that allow expression of mEmerald-labeled Lifeact under control of different promoters.
source: With this vector, three transformation-ready derivates were created that allow expression of mEmerald-labeled Lifeact under control of either the tubulin alpha 1-like protein (Siebert et al., 2008), the zerknüllt 1 (van der Zee et al., 2005; ; Sharma et al., 2013; Panfilio et al., 2013; Hilbrant et al., 2016) or the actin-related protein 5 promoter.
evidence: This describes the creation of functional vectors, supported by citations for the promoters.

claim: Two more derivatives were developed that contain expression cassettes for either mEmerald-labeled beta-galactoside alpha-2,6-sialyltransferase 1 or histone H2B under control of the tubulin alpha 1-like protein promoter.
source: Additionally, we developed two more derivates that contain expression cassettes for either mEmerald-labeled beta-galactoside alpha-2,6-sialyltransferase 1 or histone H2B under control of the tubulin alpha 1-like protein promoter.
evidence: This describes the creation of additional functional vectors.

claim: Five functional lines with a total of 13 sublines were created.
source: With these vectors, we created five functional lines with one, three, two, three and four sublines, respectively (that is, 13 in total), which are primarily designed for fluorescence live imaging.
evidence: This reports the number of functional lines created.

claim: Twelve of the 13 functional sublines went through the procedure successfully.
source: Twelve of these sublines went through the procedure successfully, only the AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 subline turned out to be heterozygous/homozygous sterile (Supplementary file 6 for the mEmerald-labeled Lifeact-expressing sublines and Supplementary file 7 for the mEmerald-labeled beta-galactoside alpha-2,6-sialyltransferase 1- and histone H2B-expressing sublines).
evidence: This reports the success rate of the procedure with functional lines, with data in Supplementary files 6 and 7.

claim: The AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 subline is heterozygous/homozygous sterile.
source: Twelve of these sublines went through the procedure successfully, only the AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 subline turned out to be heterozygous/homozygous sterile (Supplementary file 6 for the mEmerald-labeled Lifeact-expressing sublines and Supplementary file 7 for the mEmerald-labeled beta-galactoside alpha-2,6-sialyltransferase 1- and histone H2B-expressing sublines).
evidence: This reports a specific outcome for one subline, documented in Supplementary file 7.

claim: Long-term fluorescence live imaging of embryonic development was performed with three functional homozygous sublines.
source: We performed long-term fluorescence live imaging of the embryonic development (Strobl and Stelzer, 2016) with three of the functional (mC/mC) homozygous sublines.
evidence: This describes the application of the created lines, with a citation to the imaging method.

claim: A digital scanned laser light-sheet-based fluorescence microscope was used for imaging.
source: We used a digital scanned laser light-sheet-based fluorescence microscope (Keller et al., 2008; Keller and Stelzer, 2010) in conjunction with previously published sample preparation protocols for Tribolium (Strobl and Stelzer, 2014; Strobl et al., 2015; Strobl et al., 2017a).
evidence: This describes the imaging method used, supported by citations.

claim: The AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline allows characterization of actin dynamics within certain extra-embryonic membrane progenitor cells during gastrulation.
source: The AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline allows the characterization of actin dynamics within certain extra-embryonic membrane progenitor cells during gastrulation, visualizing the actomyosin cable that closes the serosa window (Figure 4A and Video 1).
evidence: This describes the application and results of one functional line, shown in Figure 4A and Video 1.

claim: The AGOC{ARP5'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1 subline provides strong fluorescence signal in the brain and ventral nerve cord and moderate signal throughout the remaining embryonic tissue.
source: The AGOC{ARP5'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1 subline provides strong fluorescence signal in the brain and ventral nerve cord and moderate signal throughout the remaining embryonic tissue (Figure 4B and Video 2).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of one functional line, shown in Figure 4B and Video 2.

claim: The AGOC{ARP5'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline provides uniform fluorescence intensity during gastrulation, germband elongation, germband retraction and dorsal closure.
source: In contrast, the AGOC{ARP5'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline provides uniform fluorescence intensity during gastrulation, germband elongation, germband retraction and dorsal closure (Figure 4C and Video 3).
evidence: This describes the expression pattern of one functional line, shown in Figure 4C and Video 3.

claim: The AGOC vector concept avoids temporary ambiguities in any generation because all genotypes are directly identified by specifically designed distinct phenotypes.
source: The unique feature of our approach is that temporary ambiguities are avoided in any generation, since all genotypes are directly identified by specifically designed distinct phenotypes.
evidence: This is a key advantage of the AGOC system as demonstrated in the study.

claim: AGOC-based workflows can be used to systematically create progeny with relevant genotypes.
source: Hence, AGOC-based workflows can be used to systematically create progeny with relevant genotypes, as exemplified in this study for the creation of homozygous lines.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The AGOC approach saves manpower compared to genetic assays.
source: (i) Our approach saves manpower. For example, genotyping 30 to 40 Tribolium adults with genetic assays takes about one afternoon (Strobl et al., 2017b), while processing the same number of individuals with a stereo microscope takes less than ten minutes.
evidence: This is a comparison of time requirements, supported by a citation for the genetic assay method.

claim: Genotyping 30 to 40 Tribolium adults with genetic assays takes about one afternoon.
source: For example, genotyping 30 to 40 Tribolium adults with genetic assays takes about one afternoon (Strobl et al., 2017b), while processing the same number of individuals with a stereo microscope takes less than ten minutes.
evidence: This is a time estimate for traditional methods, supported by a citation.

claim: Processing 30 to 40 Tribolium adults with a stereo microscope using the AGOC approach takes less than ten minutes.
source: For example, genotyping 30 to 40 Tribolium adults with genetic assays takes about one afternoon (Strobl et al., 2017b), while processing the same number of individuals with a stereo microscope takes less than ten minutes.
evidence: This is a time estimate for the AGOC method based on the authors' experience.

claim: The AGOC concept does not require any further consumables beyond standard methods.
source: (ii) The concept does not require any further consumables.
evidence: This is an advantage of the AGOC system compared to genetic assays.

claim: The AGOC concept supports unsynchronized genotyping of single organisms.
source: (iii) When genetic assays are used, the 'slowest' member of a group defines the earliest convenient time point for synchronized genotyping, while our concept also supports unsynchronized genotyping of single organisms.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the AGOC system over genetic assays.

claim: The AGOC approach is non-invasive.
source: (iv) Our approach is non-invasive and thus favorable when invasive procedures are incompatible with the experimental workflow.
evidence: This describes a key advantage of the AGOC system.

claim: The AGOC concept can be performed when sufficient amounts of genomic DNA cannot be obtained without severely injuring or sacrificing the individual.
source: It can be performed even when sufficient amounts of genomic DNA cannot be obtained without severely injuring or even sacrificing the individual.
evidence: This describes a situation where the AGOC system has an advantage over genetic assays.

claim: The AGOC concept simplifies transgenic organism handling since genotypes are determined directly.
source: (v) The concept simplifies transgenic organism handling since genotypes are determined directly.
evidence: This is an advantage of the AGOC system.

claim: Quick and reliable quantification, selection, mating and/or grouping of individuals can be performed during nearly all developmental stages using the AGOC approach.
source: Quick and reliable quantification, selection, mating and/or grouping of individuals can be performed during nearly all developmental stages.
evidence: This describes the flexibility of the AGOC system.

claim: The AGOC approach is less error-prone than genetic assays.
source: (vi) Our approach is less error-prone than genetic assays. In more than 300 independent instances, the progeny scores confirmed the phenotypically determined parental genotypes.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental results across all crosses.

claim: In more than 300 independent instances, the progeny scores confirmed the phenotypically determined parental genotypes.
source: In more than 300 independent instances, the progeny scores confirmed the phenotypically determined parental genotypes.
evidence: This reports the reliability of the AGOC system based on experimental data.

claim: Homozygous transgenic lines can be systematically created with slightly less waiting time using balancer chromosomes.
source: (vii) Although homozygous transgenic lines can be systematically created with slightly less waiting time by using balancer chromosomes, a convenient number of balancer lines is only available for Drosophila (Ashburner, 1989).
evidence: This is a comparison with an alternative method, supported by a citation.

claim: A convenient number of balancer lines is only available for Drosophila.
source: Although homozygous transgenic lines can be systematically created with slightly less waiting time by using balancer chromosomes, a convenient number of balancer lines is only available for Drosophila (Ashburner, 1989).
evidence: This is a limitation of the balancer chromosome approach, supported by a citation.

claim: In the balancer-based approach, the insertion location has to be known, while the AGOC approach performs properly in random and semi-random insertion assays.
source: Furthermore, in the balancer-based approach, the insertion location has to be known, while our approach performs properly in random and semi-random insertion assays.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the AGOC system over balancer chromosomes.

claim: Many special cases of transgenesis can be explicitly identified and/or attended to using the AGOC approach.
source: (viii) Many special cases of transgenesis (four cases that occurred during our study are described within the Materials and methods section) can be explicitly identified and/or attended to.
evidence: This describes an advantage of the AGOC system, with examples from the study.

claim: Specifically designed distinct phenotypes foster automation.
source: (ix) Specifically designed distinct phenotypes foster automation.
evidence: This is a potential advantage of the AGOC system.

claim: Several approaches for computer-controlled allocation of zebrafish embryos to 96-well plates have been suggested.
source: For example, several approaches for the computer-controlled allocation of zebrafish embryos to 96-well plates have been suggested (Graf et al., 2011; Mandrell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature on automation in zebrafish.

claim: Automation devices equipped with a phenotype-adapted detection unit can be used to sort organisms with different genotypes according to their markers.
source: Automation devices, equipped with a phenotype-adapted detection unit, in our case fluorescence, can be used to sort organisms with different genotypes according to their markers.
evidence: This is a proposed application of the AGOC system.

claim: The functionality of the AGOC vector concept was confirmed with Tribolium.
source: The functionality of the AGOC vector concept was confirmed with Tribolium, but due to the universality of the Cre-Lox system, it should work in all diploid model organisms.
evidence: This summarizes the experimental validation.

claim: Due to the universality of the Cre-Lox system, the AGOC concept should work in all diploid model organisms.
source: The functionality of the AGOC vector concept was confirmed with Tribolium, but due to the universality of the Cre-Lox system, it should work in all diploid model organisms.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the known properties of the Cre-Lox system.

claim: The AGOC concept should work in various insects, zebrafish, rodents, and plants.
source: These include various insects, zebrafish, rodents, and even plants.
evidence: This lists potential applications based on the universality of the Cre-Lox system.

claim: For many insect species, modifying the basic architecture of the AGOC vector is not necessary.
source: For many insect species, modifying the basic architecture of the vector is not necessary.
evidence: This is a prediction about the applicability of the AGOC system.

claim: Both the piggyBac transposon system and the 3×P3 promoter function properly in Drosophila melanogaster.
source: It has been shown that both the piggyBac transposon system and the 3×P3 promoter function properly in Drosophila melanogaster (Sarkar et al., 2006), its close relative Drosophila suzukii (Schetelig and Handler, 2013) and many other dipterans (Hediger et al., 2001; Warren et al., 2010; Caroti et al., 2015), including epidemiologically relevant mosquito species such as Aedes aegypti (Kokoza et al., 2001) and Aedes albopictus (Labbé et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to the literature.

claim: The piggyBac transposon system and 3×P3 promoter function properly in multiple lepidopterans such as Bicyclus anynana and Bombyx mori.
source: This also applies to multiple lepidopterans such as Bicyclus anynana (Marcus et al., 2004) and Bombyx mori (Thomas et al., 2002), other coleopterans (Kuwayama et al., 2006) as well as some hymenopterans, for example the honeybee Apis mellifera (Schulte et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: For several dipteran species, the marker cassettes have to be modified by replacing the 3×P3 promoter with the Drosophila polyubiquitin promoter.
source: For several other dipteran species, such as the African malaria mosquito Anopheles gambiae (Grossman et al., 2001) as well as several tephritid (Handler and Harrell, 2001; Schetelig et al., 2009; Raphael et al., 2011) and calliphorid (Heinrich et al., 2002; Allen et al., 2004) species, the marker cassettes have to be modified, for example by replacing the artificial 3×P3 promoter with the Drosophila polyubiquitin promoter.
evidence: This is a recommendation for adapting the AGOC system, supported by citations.

claim: Eye pigmentation markers are available for Drosophila melanogaster and Tribolium castaneum.
source: Eye pigmentation markers are available for Drosophila melanogaster (Adams and Sekelsky, 2002) and Tribolium castaneum (Lorenzen et al., 2002), but require the appropriate background strain.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Arylalkylamine-N-acetyl transferase-based markers lighten pigmentation throughout the cuticle and can be detected without microscopes.
source: Another convenient and apparently universal option for insects are arylalkylamine-N-acetyl transferase-based markers, which lighten pigmentation throughout the cuticle and thus can be detected without microscopes (Osanai-Futahashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: The piggyBac transposon system works properly in zebrafish.
source: Although the piggyBac transposon system works properly in zebrafish (Lobo et al., 2006) and the 3×P3 promoter is believed to work in a broad variety of animal species (Berghammer et al., 1999), it may be convenient to transit to the well-established Tol2 transposon system (Kawakami et al., 2000) and to replace the 3×P3 promoter in the marker cassettes with endogenous alternatives, for example the eye-specific cryaa or the muscle-specific 503unc promoter (Berger and Currie, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The 3×P3 promoter is believed to work in a broad variety of animal species.
source: Although the piggyBac transposon system works properly in zebrafish (Lobo et al., 2006) and the 3×P3 promoter is believed to work in a broad variety of animal species (Berghammer et al., 1999), it may be convenient to transit to the well-established Tol2 transposon system (Kawakami et al., 2000) and to replace the 3×P3 promoter in the marker cassettes with endogenous alternatives, for example the eye-specific cryaa or the muscle-specific 503unc promoter (Berger and Currie, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature.

claim: For mouse, epidermal and eye-specific fluorescence-based markers have been established.
source: For mouse, epidermal (Ikawa et al., 1995; Zhu et al., 2005) and eye-specific (Cornett et al., 2011) fluorescence-based as well as fur color-based (Zheng et al., 1999) markers have been established.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the literature.

claim: The AGOC vector concept was used in conjunction with transposon-mediated transgenesis to systematically create functional homozygous Tribolium lines designed for fluorescence live imaging.
source: In this study, we used the AGOC vector concept in conjunction with transposon-mediated transgenesis to systematically create functional homozygous Tribolium lines that are primarily designed for fluorescence live imaging of embryonic development.
evidence: This summarizes the main application demonstrated in the study.

claim: The AGOC approach can be used in insertional mutagenesis knock-out assays.
source: However, our approach can also be used in insertional mutagenesis knock-out assays, independent of whether large-scale transposon-mediated remobilization with subsequent screening is performed (Trauner et al., 2009), or genes or genetic elements are specifically rendered inoperative, for example, by using genome engineering techniques such as CRISPR/Cas9, where AGOC-based transgenes can be integrated into targeted genomic locations via either homology-based repair or non-homologous end-joining (Gilles and Averof, 2014; Gilles et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a proposed application supported by citations to relevant techniques.

claim: Studies that utilize genetically manipulated organisms require researchers to rear their lines for many years.
source: Studies that utilize genetically manipulated organisms require researchers to rear their lines for many years.
evidence: This is a statement about common practice in the field.

claim: A certain number of individuals with known genotypes are required to maintain lines or use them in experiments, resulting in a total demand of hundreds to thousands of organisms.
source: A certain numbers of individuals with known genotypes are required during this period, either to maintain the lines or to use them in experiments. This results in a total demand of hundreds to thousands of organisms.
evidence: This is a statement about the practical requirements of maintaining transgenic lines.

claim: Transgenic lines designed for fluorescence live imaging are easily maintained as homozygotes using the AGOC concept since continuous genotyping and/or curation are not necessary.
source: (i) Transgenic lines that are, for example, specifically designed for fluorescence live imaging are easily maintained as homozygotes since continuous genotyping and/or curation are not necessary.
evidence: This is an advantage of the AGOC system for maintaining lines.

claim: The initial workload following transgenesis required to create homozygous lines can be very high and a limiting factor.
source: However, the initial workload following transgenesis that is required to create homozygous lines can be very high and thus a limiting factor.
evidence: This describes a challenge in traditional methods.

claim: The efforts to create homozygous lines are significantly reduced by using the AGOC vector concept.
source: As shown in this study, these efforts are significantly reduced by using the AGOC vector concept.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: In knock-out assays of genes that result in homozygous lethality, the respective lines are maintained as hemizygotes, which are usually viable and phenotypically inconspicuous.
source: (ii) In knock-out assays of genes that result in homozygous lethality, the respective lines are maintained as hemizygotes, which are usually viable and phenotypically inconspicuous.
evidence: This describes standard practice for maintaining lethal knock-out lines.

claim: When two hemizygous organisms are mated, only one quarter of their progeny are homozygous for the knock-out, while half are hemizygous and one quarter resemble the wild type.
source: When two hemizygous organisms are mated, only one quarter of their progeny are homozygous for the knock-out, while half are hemizygous and one quarter resemble the wild type.
evidence: This describes the expected Mendelian ratios for such crosses.

claim: By using the AGOC approach with appropriate markers, a preselection can be performed that narrows efforts down to relevant individuals and appropriate controls.
source: By using our approach with appropriate markers, a preselection can be performed. This narrows the efforts down to relevant individuals and appropriate controls, for example, down to about one quarter of the currently required number.
evidence: This is a proposed application that would reduce the number of animals needed.

claim: The AGOC vector concept contributes to ethically motivated endeavors to minimize the number of wasted animals.
source: The AGOC vector concept, broadly adapted to established and emerging model organisms, contributes significantly to ethically motivated endeavors to minimize the number of wasted animals.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the ethical implications of the AGOC system.

claim: A T. castaneum double mutant background strain was created that carries the pearl and light ocular diaphragm mutations resulting in completely unpigmented eyes.
source: For this study, a T. castaneum (NCBITaxon:7070) double mutant background strain was created, which carries the pearl (Grubbs et al., 2015) and light ocular diaphragm (Mocelin and Stuart, 1996) mutations that result in completely unpigmented eyes.
evidence: This describes the creation of a background strain, supported by citations.

claim: The double mutant background strain was called Plain-White-As-Snow (PWAS).
source: This strain was called Plain-White-As-Snow (PWAS) and used as a donor for genomic DNA and messenger RNA as well as for the creation of transgenic lines.
evidence: This reports the naming and use of the background strain.

claim: The pAVOIAF{#1–#2–#3–#4} vector carries a transposon cassette between unique AatII and PciI sites.
source: Between the unique AatII and PciI sites, this vector carries a transposon cassette which consists of (i) the piggyBac 3' terminal repeat, (ii) a four-slot (#1 to #4) cloning site and (iii) the 5' piggyBac terminal repeat.
evidence: This describes the vector design.

claim: The piggyBac terminal repeats have the minimal length necessary for efficient transposition.
source: The repeats have the minimal length (235 and 310 bp, respectively) necessary for efficient transposition (Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the literature on piggyBac transposition.

claim: In the AGOC #4 subline, incomplete recombination occurred in the F4 double hemizygous generation.
source: *In the AGOC #4 subline, incomplete recombination occurred in the F4 (mCe; mO-mC) double hemizygous generation, as we obtained several F5 individuals that still carried both transformation markers (7.0% in total).
evidence: This reports an experimental observation for one subline.

claim: The mating procedure was continued with the F5 post-recombination hemizygous progeny for the AGOC #4 subline despite incomplete recombination.
source: We continued the mating procedure with the F5 (mO) and (mC) post-recombination hemizygous progeny.
evidence: This describes how the researchers handled the incomplete recombination case.

claim: The transgenes of AGOC #3, AGOC{ATub'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1, and AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 sublines are heterozygous/homozygous lethal.
source: The homozygous viability crosses indicated that the transgenes of the proof-of-principle AGOC #3, the functional AGOC{ATub'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1 and the functional AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 sublines are heterozygous/homozygous lethal (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This reports experimental results documented in Supplementary file 2.

claim: F6 heterozygotes were obtained for AGOC #3, AGOC{ATub'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1, and AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 sublines despite heterozygous/homozygous lethality.
source: However, F6 (mO/mC) heterozygotes were obtained for all three lines and the mating procedure could be performed successfully with the AGOC #3 and AGOC{ATub'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1 sublines (Table 1, Supplementary file 6 and Supplementary file 7).
evidence: This reports experimental results showing the procedure could still work.

claim: The mating procedure aborted for the AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 subline because F6 heterozygotes were sterile.
source: The mating procedure only aborted for the AGOC{ATub'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #4 subline, because the F6 (mO/mC) heterozygotes were sterile.
evidence: This reports the outcome for one subline where the procedure failed.

claim: Hemizygous individuals of AGOC #3, AGOC{ATub'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1, and AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 are believed to be exposed to high stress levels.
source: Since the transgene of the proof-of-principle AGOC #3 subline might interfere with the sialin-like gene due to its insertion location (Supplementary file 3), and since both functional sublines mentioned above display a strong green fluorescence signal, hemizygous individuals of those three sublines are believed to be exposed to high stress levels, and that these levels are even higher in homozygotes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The transgenic sublines AGOC #3, AGOC{ATub'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #1, and AGOC{ATub'H2B-mEmerald} #4 are believed to be essentially viable, but a certain percentage of descendants fail to develop properly.
source: Thus, these transgenic sublines are believed to be essentially viable, but a certain percentage of the descendants fail to develop properly, which results in biased progeny ratios in the homozygous viability cross.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results.

claim: The AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline carries the transgene on the X allosome.
source: (iii) The AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline carries the transgene not on one of the nine autosomes, but on the X allosome.
evidence: This reports a special case observed in one subline.

claim: A slightly modified mating procedure was necessary to obtain F7 homozygotes for the AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #2 subline.
source: Thus, a slightly modified mating procedure was necessary to obtain F7 (mO/mO) and (mC/mC) homozygotes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This describes how the procedure was adapted for an X-linked transgene.

claim: In the AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #3 subline, an insertion of the transgene into the backbone of another vector occurred.
source: (iv) The piggyBac transposon system is highly efficient in Tribolium, which results to a certain degree also from the 4 bp TTAA target sequence. However, due to this very short length of the targeting sequence, a certain probability for nested insertions is given, that is, the transgene inserts into another transformation vector, since these vectors also carry multiple TTAA target sequences. In the AGOC{Zen1'#O(LA)-mEmerald} #3 subline, an insertion of the transgene into the backbone of another vector occurred, and the nested transgene was subsequently inserted into the genome, as revealed by sequencing of the insertion junction (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This reports a special case observed in one subline, confirmed by sequencing.

claim: The nested insertion case is 'corrected' during the AGOC mating procedure because Cre recombinase excises nearly one 'stitched equivalent' of the initial transformation vector from the genome.
source: This rare and undesired case is 'corrected' during the mating procedure of the AGOC vector concept, since within the F4 (mCe; mO-mC) double hemizygous generation, the Cre recombinase excises nearly one 'stitched equivalent' of the initial transformation vector from the genome.
evidence: This explains how the AGOC system handles nested insertions.

claim: All shown embryos survived the imaging procedure and developed to healthy and fertile adults.
source: All shown embryos survived the imaging procedure, developed to healthy and fertile adults, and when mated with wild types, produced only transgenic progeny that were also fertile.
evidence: This reports the viability of imaged embryos.

claim: Imaged embryos that developed to adults produced only transgenic progeny when mated with wild types.
source: All shown embryos survived the imaging procedure, developed to healthy and fertile adults, and when mated with wild types, produced only transgenic progeny that were also fertile.
evidence: This confirms the homozygous nature of the imaged lines.
